lines.text: September 1967. A three year old Appaloosa mare walks out into a pasture in southern Colorado. Two days later she is found dead, and her head is picked clean to the bone.
Newspapers across America said she was killed by a flying saucer. A pathologist said the cuts were too clean for any animal. A sheriff said it was lightning.
So tonight we open this as an inquest. Six exhibits. Every claim called as a witness, and cross examined.
Who was the horse? What exactly was found? What do the experts say? And why did a few hundred cattle in the years after seem to die the same way?
At the end, a verdict. Unexplained, explained, or a legend that grew faster than the facts. Court is in session.
Exhibit A. The victim. Her name was Lady. A young Appaloosa mare, owned by Nellie Lewis, and pastured on her brother Harry King's ranch near Alamosa.
The King ranch sits in the San Luis Valley, a high flat basin more than seven thousand feet up, ringed by the Sangre de Cristo mountains.
Harry King and his wife Agnes ran cattle there. In early September the mare did not come in. On the seventh, she was simply gone.
They searched the pasture. Nothing. The grass was dry, the ground firm. Two days later, on September ninth, Agnes and Harry walked out and found her.
She lay on her side in a patch of flattened brush. And from a distance, Harry said later, it looked like something was wrong with her head.
The Pueblo Chieftain ran the story. The wire services picked it up. And somewhere along the way the horse got a different name.
Reporters called her Snippy. That was actually the name of her sire, a horse owned by Berle Lewis. The wrong name stuck, and so did the mystery.
Exhibit B. The body. The head and neck were stripped of flesh, down to clean white bone, as if cut away along a line at the shoulder.
The rest of the body was intact. No blood on the ground. No drag marks. No tracks of people or vehicles, according to the family.
Around her, six round marks in the ground, about two inches across and four inches deep, set in a circle roughly three feet wide. The brush around her was pressed flat.
A forest service man, Duane Martin, reportedly passed a Geiger counter over the spot. The needle, he said, read higher near the body than elsewhere.
That detail would be repeated for decades. It also came from a handheld instrument, a single reading, and no record of calibration.
And then people came. Carloads of them. Reporters, sightseers, ufo fans. By the time anyone competent looked, the ground had been trampled flat.
Locals also talked of strange lights over the valley that autumn. The flying saucer story had arrived, and it fit the shape of the times.
Exhibit C. The sheriff. Ben Phillips of Alamosa County looked at the case and gave a flat answer. The mare, he said, was struck by lightning.
Lightning does kill horses. It leaves burns on the skin and sometimes singes the ground. It does not strip a head to the bone. And he never visited the site.
Then came Doctor John Altshuler, a Denver pathologist. He looked at the remains years later, and his account became the centre of the legend.
He said the cut at the neck was clean, almost cauterized, like a surgical incision. He said the heart, lungs and thyroid were gone, and the brain looked unusually clean.
In 1967 the Associated Press quoted him saying organs were missing, and that it was definitely not lightning. His later, bigger claims came decades after.
Now the other side. An independent veterinary pathologist for the University of Colorado, working for the Air Force project, saw the same horse differently.
The government project was run by physicist Edward Condon at the University of Colorado. Snippy is Case thirty two in its final report, written in 1968.
Let's hear what the Condon team's own investigators actually found. Because it is not what the flying saucer version leaves out.
Exhibit D. The cross examination. Investigator Wadsworth Ayer reached the case after the crowds. First fact: hundreds of visitors had trampled the site.
Second fact. The vet found a severe infection in one hind leg. The mare may have been lame, sick and in pain for some time before she died.
Third fact. A knife cut in the neck. His working idea: someone may have found her suffering and put her down, which is legal on a ranch.
Fourth fact, and the strangest one. Magpies. Those birds will strip soft flesh from a carcass in days, and they favour an opened neck or wound.
The skin and muscle go first from the head. What you are left with is a clean, pale skull that can look cut from a distance.
As for the missing organs: the investigators said that in a body found days after death, the soft organs are often gone or rotted. That is normal.
The pressed brush and six round marks? The team noted that the horse's body, and its struggles, could flatten brush, and the marks were not specific.
Their conclusion in the Condon report was blunt. No evidence of abnormal causes. No evidence of anything beyond predators, decay, and a sick horse.
Does that settle it? Not quite. Doctor Altshuler's own account still disagrees with the report. Two honest accounts, decades apart, of the same remains.
And that, says every honest researcher, is the problem. The one body that really mattered was gone, buried, and never tested to modern standards.
Exhibit E. The panic. Within weeks, ranchers across Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska and the Dakotas began to report cattle found dead, oddly stripped.
Some said ears, tongues, udders and sex organs were removed, with no blood and no tracks. Whole towns started watching the sky at night.
Farmers sat up with rifles. Sheriffs formed patrols. A Colorado state official called the cases a wave of unexplained mutilations.
Black helicopters were reported. Strange lights. Unmarked vans. The story grew a government villain, and then an alien one.
By the nineteen seventies the Federal Bureau of Investigation and state police had hundreds of reports on their desks.
In nineteen seventy nine the FBI's Kenneth Rommel investigated New Mexico cases for the Senate. His team put the cause as predators and decay.
Scavengers can take eyes, tongues, lips and soft parts first. And blowflies soften skin edges, so the cuts can look like a scalpel did them.
Researchers who studied the cases, including a dedicated Colorado investigation, found no pattern that predators and ordinary decay could not explain.
Exhibit F. The theories. Theory one, the popular one: extraterrestrials harvesting tissue from Earth animals, for study, or for food.
Theory two: satanic cults, performing rituals on animals. A real panic of the era. Investigators found no cult, no evidence, no arrests tied to the cases.
Theory three: a secret government programme testing something on cattle, from germ warfare to radiation. Rumours only. No documents have ever shown it.
Theory four: fallout. Cold war nuclear testing worried farmers everywhere, and a Geiger counter in a story felt like proof. It was not.
Theory five, the quiet one: nothing happened. Normal deaths, normal predators, and an alarmed public primed by the saucer craze to read patterns into them.
Social scientists call it a moral panic. Reports surge after a famous story, then fade. The mutilation wave rose and fell with newspaper coverage.
And the legend never died. In the San Luis Valley a roadside tourist attraction still draws visitors, and the story was revived in the news in twenty twenty two.
The court has heard everything. Time to weigh the evidence, exhibit by exhibit, and give the case its score.
The inquest asks the same three questions about each claim. Is it documented? Is it independent? And does the simpler explanation fit?
First, the part we cannot answer. We never saw the original data from Altshuler's examination. The remains were buried. No tissue was ever stored.
Second, the fact that matters. The one place where the legend started, Lady, has a plain explanation that fits every observation we can check.
Remember what she was. A sick young horse, in pain, on a ranch where someone may have ended her suffering, and nature did the rest.
Why does it feel so unsatisfying? Because a plain explanation arrives long after the exciting one, and never gets the headlines.
Debrief. Time to score the case of Snippy the horse.

A real horse, found dead in September nineteen sixty seven, her head stripped to bone: evidence. Magpies, infection, and a knife cut: documented in the Condon report. Trampled site and one early Geiger reading: weak.
Alien surgery: no evidence. A cult or secret government lab: no evidence. A national wave of mutilations as a news driven panic: well supported. One honest unknown, the lost original remains.
The verdict. Explained, as far as the evidence reaches. A sick horse, scavengers and a panic. The saucers were never needed. But the buried truth keeps the legend alive.
Somewhere in Colorado, a family lost a horse and woke up the next day in the middle of a national story. They never asked for any of it.
Next case: one night, one radio telescope, and a signal so strong the astronomer wrote one word beside it. Was it the first message from another world?
What do you think happened to Lady? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
